label: frost

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Frost. The central flower petals are dark brown to black, the receptacle is shriveled and blackened, the surrounding green sepals are slightly wilted, and the blossom edges show a dull, water-soaked look rather than the usual glossy sheen. These color changes and tissue collapse indicate that the flower was exposed to a brief but intense freeze that killed the reproductive tissue while leaving the foliage intact. To protect future blooms, drape a breathable row cover or lightweight fleece over the bed each evening when forecasts dip below 2 °C (36 °F), and add a 5 cm (2 in) layer of clean straw mulch around the crown to trap and slow radiating heat. Irrigate to a depth of 2.5 cm (1 in) before the next predicted freeze to release stored heat, and remove dead flowers with sanitized scissors to reduce inoculum. Over the next seven days, visually check each morning for new blackened centers on open flowers, note any fresh wilting or yellowing of leaves, and verify that the mulch remains dry to the touch by midday to confirm protection is working.

label: root_rot

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Root rot. The lower crown tissue is dark brown-black and water-soaked, the outer root tips appear mushy and discolored, the inner cortex shows a pale, water-soaked band, and the overall root mass is sparse with few white feeder roots, all indicating decay rather than Healthy white tissue. These visual clues point to roots suffocating in saturated, poorly aerated media that favors soil-borne fungi such as Phytophthora or Pythium. Immediately lift plants onto a 15 cm-high raised bed or mound, mix in 30 % coarse compost or sand to improve drainage, and irrigate only when the top 2 cm of soil is dry, delivering about 2 cm of water early in the morning so foliage dries quickly. Remove and discard the most visibly affected plants and sanitize tools with 10 % bleach solution for 1 minute between cuts. Over the next week, check daily that soil at 5 cm depth remains moist but not soggy, gently probe the crown for firmness rather than mushiness, and watch for emergence of new white root tips at the crown base as signs of recovery.

label: frost

attempts.report: The leaf surface shows irregular patches of tan-brown tissue, the margins are slightly curled inward, the achenes are slightly sunken and pale, and the overall texture is dull and matte rather than glossy. These discolored patches are concentrated on the upper half of the leaflet, indicating cold injury rather than pathogen spread. The damage is localized and stops at the petiole junction, suggesting overnight temperature fluctuations rather than pathogen progression. To reduce future damage, apply a 5–7 cm (2–3 in) layer of clean straw mulch around the crown, irrigate to a depth of 2.5 cm (1 in) before the next predicted frost, and install a 30–40 % shade cloth 40 cm (16 in) above the canopy during the coldest hours. Improve airflow by trimming excess runners and removing dead leaves, and if forecasts predict temperatures below –2 °C (28 °F), drape a breathable floating row cover to trap warmth. Over the next seven days, inspect each morning for new brown lesions spreading beyond the current patches, check that soil stays moist but not waterlogged, and confirm that the mulch remains dry to the touch by midday to verify protection is working.

label: root_rot

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Root rot. The main crown shows a dark, water-soaked band 3–5 mm wide along the outer surface, the outer 1–2 cm of fine feeder roots are missing or blackened, and the remaining roots appear stringy and brittle rather than firm and white. These clues point to prolonged saturation that favors soil-borne fungi causing rot in the root zone. Immediately lift the plant onto a raised bed or mound 20–25 cm high and incorporate 5 cm of coarse compost or perlite into the top 15 cm of soil to improve drainage; thereafter irrigate only when the upper 3 cm of soil is dry, supplying about 2 cm of water in the early morning so moisture can penetrate to at least 10 cm depth. Remove any dead or mushy roots with sterilized scissors and discard them away from the bed, and space plants 30 cm apart to enhance airflow. Over the next week, probe soil daily at 5 cm depth to confirm it is moist but not wet, watch for emergence of firm, white root tips at the crown edge, and note any new leaf wilting or yellowing as an early sign of further rot progression.

label: gray_mold

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Gray mold. Several berries show a dull gray-brown fuzz on the surface, the calyx of one fruit is shriveled and brown, and several adjacent berries appear water-soaked and soft, all concentrated where straw mulch contacts the fruit. These clues point to Botrytis cinerea thriving in stagnant, humid pockets created by dense foliage and wet berries touching the soil. Immediately clip and discard every affected berry and any touching debris, then thin the canopy so that at least 10 cm (4 in) of open space surrounds each cluster and keep the mulch dry; irrigate only at the base with 2–3 cm (1 in) of water once every 4–5 days in early morning to keep fruit dry. Lay a clean 5 cm (2 in) layer of straw or plastic mulch under the trusses to keep fruit off damp soil and improve airflow. Over the next seven days, inspect daily for new gray fuzz on calyxes, check that berries remain firm and dry rather than soft or water-soaked, and verify that leaf surfaces are dry within two hours after watering or dew.

These clues point to prolonged surface moisture and poor airflow that allowed spores to germinate and spread from touching fruit. attempts.report: Diagnosis: Gray mold. The fruit surface is uniformly dark brown to almost black, with a dull sheen and a distinct water-soaked margin that has turned tan-brown; the calyx end shows a faint gray fuzz, and the surrounding tissue is shriveled and papery, all consistent with Botrytis cinerea infection. Spores are visible in the center of the lesion, and the mold appears to have colonized the soft, water-exposed skin rather than the hard seed core. Thinning the surrounding foliage and removing fallen petals or debris that could harbor spores is the first step, then irrigate only at soil level early in the morning with 2–3 cm (≈1 in) of water once every 5–7 days to keep the fruit dry. Improve airflow by trimming excess runners and keeping plants spaced at least 25 cm (10 in) apart, and gently squeeze the fruit to remove any moldy tissue before harvesting. Over the next week, inspect daily for new gray fuzz on calyx ends, check that soil dries to the top 5 cm (2 in) after each watering, and note any fresh brown lesions that expand beyond 5 mm in diameter, removing them immediately to prevent spore spread.

label: root_rot

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Root rot. The crown and primary roots are dark brown to almost black, with a soft, water-soaked texture rather than the expected creamy white; many fine feeder roots are missing or shriveled, leaving a sparse, brittle root mass; the remaining roots are slimy and stringy, indicating decay; the soil surface is saturated and matted, suggesting prolonged waterlogging; and the plant shows a sudden loss of vigor with wilted leaves and a thin, pale stem. These clues point to root rot caused by persistent soil moisture and poor drainage that favors soil-borne fungi such as Phytophthora or Pythium. Immediately improve drainage by raising the bed 15–20 cm and blending in 30 % coarse sand or perlite to reduce waterlogging; irrigate only when the top 3 cm of soil is dry, applying no more than 2.5 cm of water in a single early-morning session; and remove all dead roots with sterilized shears to open the root system to airflow. Mulch lightly (2–3 cm) after drying to prevent surface crusting but keep it 2 cm away from the crown to improve airflow. Over the next seven days, check daily for any new blackening or sliminess at the crown base, probe soil moisture at 5 cm depth to ensure it stays moist but not wet, and observe the appearance of new white root tips emerging from the crown; if any of these indicators worsen, repeat sanitation and drainage adjustments immediately.

label: frost

attempts.report: Diagnosis: Frost Injury. The plant shows a dense cluster of young leaves with several uniformly dark-brown, necrotic patches along the margins, a few slightly wilted leaf tips, and overall dull, slightly yellowed coloration, all concentrated on the lower half of the canopy. These symptoms are consistent with cold injury from recent frosts that burned the most exposed tissue. Frosts can also cause water-soaked lesions that later turn brown, as seen here. Prolonged exposure to cold temperatures can disrupt nutrient uptake and trigger secondary infections, so immediate action is needed to protect the plant. First, move the pot or bed into a protected area with at least 50 % shade during the coldest hours (e.g., morning sun) and ensure good airflow; second, apply a 3–4 cm (1.2–1.6 in) layer of mulch around the crown to buffer soil temperature; third, water the root zone only when the top 2 cm (¾ in) of soil feels dry, supplying about 2.5 cm (1 in) of water early in the morning to reduce evaporation; and finally, if night temperatures are forecast below 2 °C (35 °F), cover the plant with a breathable row cover or lightweight blanket to trap radiant heat. Over the next seven days, check daily for new brown patches expanding beyond the current damage, monitor soil moisture with a finger test to ensure it stays moist but not waterlogged, and confirm that foliage regains a brighter green color by midday after each frost event.
